capabilities.target: Customer refund via payments processor, any order, up to order total

inputs.source: Support staff refund request via SSO-authenticated channel

instructions.note: The agent may issue a refund for any order and any amount up to the order total, and is told to 'use your judgment on partial refunds,' with no per-staff authorization tiers or amount thresholds defined.
'Check the order, then issue the refund' is the only stated safeguard, and it is enforced solely by the model's own behavior; 'Do not ask for confirmation' explicitly removes any human gate.
'Use your judgment on partial refunds' gives no criteria for when a partial versus full refund is appropriate.

elements.name: Refund issuance to payments processor / customer

controls.name: Check the order before issuing a refund (prompt instruction)
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model's own judgment to verify the order before refunding, worded ambiguously ('use your judgment' on partial refunds); a more capable or longer-running model can rationalize skipping or misapplying the check, and the instruction gives no objective verification criteria.

controls.name: Attributable, tamper-evident logging of requesting staff identity for refund actions
Per-staff or aggregate rate/spend limit on refund issuance
Per-staff or role-scoped credentials for refund and order-read capabilities
Human approval gate (raw action review) for refunds above a defined threshold

findings.title: Missing attributable provenance for refund actions (repudiation)

forecast.watch_signal: Any widening of who can request refunds, or removal of SSO authentication, without first adding per-staff attributable, tamper-evident logging tied to the refund action.

evidence.observation: The processor log records the service account, amount, and order, but not which staff member asked or why; staff chats are deleted after 7 days, so no attributable record of who requested a given refund survives.

recommendations.action: Record the authenticated staff member's identity (not just the shared service account) with every refund action in a tamper-evident log that is retained independently of the ephemeral staff chat history.

findings.title: No rate or spend limit on refund issuance (denial of wallet / cost harvesting)

forecast.watch_signal: Any increase in refund request volume per staff member per day, or any change that lets a single workflow trigger multiple refunds in sequence without a cumulative cap.

evidence.observation: The prompt says 'Do not ask for confirmation,' and no max_unattended_steps, max_runtime_minutes, or daily/aggregate spend cap on refund issuance is described; refunds are irreversible once settled, usually within a day, so a burst of erroneous or abusive refunds cannot be clawed back.

recommendations.action: Add a per-staff and/or aggregate daily rate or spend cap on refund issuance, enforced outside the model, with alerting as thresholds are approached.

findings.title: Shared service account grants every staff request full refund privilege (confused deputy / elevation of privilege)

forecast.watch_signal: Any addition of new support tools or staff roles sharing the same service account, or any relaxation that lets more staff trigger refunds without per-role authorization limits.

evidence.observation: The agent calls the payments processor with one shared service account used by every support tool, and the prompt gives no indication that refund authority varies by the requesting staff member's role, seniority, or amount threshold ('Process refund requests from support staff... Use your judgment on partial refunds').

recommendations.action: Replace the single shared service account with per-staff or role-scoped credentials so the agent's effective authority matches the requester's actual refund authorization.
Require a raw-action human approval gate, reviewed individually, for refunds above a defined amount threshold.

stride_coverage.rationale: No external peer agents or MCP servers interact with this agent; staff authenticate via SSO before their requests reach it, so there is no spoofable agent identity in this single-agent design.
can_modify_own_config is false, and no mechanism for altering the agent's own instructions, tools, or definitions at runtime is described in these artifacts.

The only recipient of order and payment data is the payments processor itself, the intended counterparty for processing the refund; no untrusted source or additional egress channel is present that could disclose this data elsewhere.

The refund destination is the customer's payment method already on file with the order; the design gives no mechanism for a requester to redirect funds to an arbitrary destination, so there is no spoofable external recipient identity to assess.
This external entity is solely the passive recipient of refund payments; it does not initiate actions within this design that would need to be attributed or that could be repudiated.
The artifacts do not state whether the processor log is append-only, write-once, or otherwise protected from modification; integrity controls on the log itself are not described.
The artifacts do not describe who can read the processor log or what access controls apply to the amounts, orders, and service-account entries it contains.
The log is maintained by the payments processor itself as a standard transaction record; this design grants the agent no capability that could exhaust or disable that logging service.
Transport-level integrity protections (e.g., TLS, request signing) between the agent and the payments processor API are not described in these artifacts.
Transport confidentiality protections for the refund call to the payments processor are not described in these artifacts.

rating.rationale: No untrusted source reaches the refund or order-read capabilities today; all three findings are property findings (rubric 5a) arising from an irreversible, S3-class spend capability (cap.issue_refund) operated via a single shared service account, with no per-staff attribution in the processor log, no rate or spend cap, no per-staff authorization scoping, and full A4 autonomy ('do not ask for confirmation'). Each finding's inherent tier is the I-row S3 base (high) raised one tier by the A4 autonomy modifier and capped at high per rubric 5a. No declared control restores any of the three missing properties (SSO authentication identifies the requester but is not propagated into the audit trail; the 'check the order' instruction is behavioral and unrelated to attribution, rate limits, or authorization scoping), so residual equals inherent at high for all three. Forecast also holds at high because the property-finding ceiling, not an active control, is what currently bounds the tier; the gaps are structural today, not decaying controls. The single highest-leverage fix is adding attributable, tamper-evident logging of the requesting staff member (missing control c.attributable_logging), closing the repudiation gap and the lack of accountability that compounds the other two findings.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in prompt.md and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No MCP/tool manifest or IaC was provided; credential_scope, data_sensitivity, and egress properties of the capabilities are inferred from the prompt and runtime notes rather than verified against actual system configuration, so confidence is medium.
The artifacts do not describe who can read the payments processor log or whether it is tamper-evident, so those STRIDE categories on store.processor_log are marked not_assessed rather than scored.
